title: Prayer, Power and Woes at Table
sum: A disciple watches Jesus pray and asks to be taught. Jesus gives a short form of the Lord's Prayer, then a parable about a friend who knocks at midnight and a promise: the Father in heaven will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. When he drives a demon out of a speechless man, some say he works by Beelzebul and others demand a sign. He answers that he drives out demons by the finger of God, so God's kingdom has arrived; that a stronger man has come to plunder the strong one; and that an emptied life must be filled.

A woman blesses his mother; he blesses those who hear the word of God and keep it. To the growing crowds he says the only sign will be the sign of Jonah, and warns them to check whether their light is darkness. At a Pharisee's meal his host is surprised that he does not wash first, and Jesus answers with three woes on the Pharisees and three on the lawyers. The meal ends in open hostility, with scribes and Pharisees hunting for a word to use against him.
readings: Read as a lesson in prayer and hearing

The chapter moves from praying (11:1–13) to hearing (11:14–36) to doing (11:37–54). The disciples ask how to pray and are taught to trust a generous Father. The crowds hear Jesus' works and words and must decide what they mean. The Pharisees and lawyers keep every outward rule but miss justice and the love of God. The hinge is 11:28: blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.

From 11:14 the chapter is a mounting conflict: an accusation of sorcery, a demand for a sign, a host's disapproval, a lawyer's protest, and finally a plot. Luke shows that Jesus' opponents were not only in Jerusalem but in the towns of Galilee and the journey, and that the cross was the end of a long road of rejection, as the prophets' deaths had been (11:47–51).

Almost everything in the chapter is at home in first-century Judaism: a prayer that echoes the Kaddish, Jewish exorcists, the finger of God from the exodus, Jonah's Nineveh as the model of repentance, and debates about purity, tithes and graves. Jewish readers such as Amy-Jill Levine ask Christians to see the woes as an argument inside Judaism, like the prophets' rebukes, not as a verdict on Jews or Judaism as a whole.

views.H: Galilean village life lies behind the friend at midnight (one-room houses, shared bread, hospitality as village honor). Jewish exorcists like Eleazar in Josephus explain "your sons" (11:19). The woes reflect real Pharisaic practice: tithing herbs, hand-washing before meals, the inner and outer surfaces of vessels, marked graves, and the monumental tombs of Herodian Jerusalem.
views.C: Most of the chapter comes from the material Luke shares with Matthew, Q on the usual theory: the Lord's Prayer, ask-seek-knock, Beelzebul, the sign of Jonah, the lamp and the woes. Luke's own material is the friend at midnight and the woman in the crowd. Luke's shorter Lord's Prayer and "finger of God" are widely thought older than Matthew's wording; scholars who think Luke used Matthew directly (the Farrer theory) see deliberate abbreviation and adaptation instead.
views.L: Luke sets the teaching in scenes: a request (11:1), a healing (11:14), a woman's cry (11:27), crowds pressing in (11:29), a dinner invitation (11:37). Meals are a key setting in Luke, and this is the second of three meals with Pharisees (7:36; 14:1). Words echo across the chapter: the friend who will not get up (11:7–8) and the stronger man who comes (11:22); the light within (11:35) and the inside of the cup (11:39–41).
views.J: The prayer, the exorcisms and the arguments over purity are inner-Jewish. Luke's Pharisees are not cardboard enemies: one invites Jesus to his home, and later Pharisees warn him of Herod (13:31). The woes repeat the prophets' style of rebuke (Isaiah 5:8–23; Amos 6:1). Christian preaching has often used 11:37–54 to caricature Judaism as empty ritual, which the text, set in a debate among Jews about purity and justice, does not support.
views.T: The Lord's Prayer became the church's prayer, mostly in Matthew's form. Origen and Tertullian wrote whole treatises on it. Luke's promise that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask (11:13) fits the church's long habit of praying for the Spirit, as in the hymn "Come, Creator Spirit" (Veni Creator Spiritus), sung at ordinations and councils since the Middle Ages, though the hymn is not drawn from this verse. In the Orthodox Church 11:27–28 is read at feasts of the Mother of God.

deep.h: Two forms of the Lord's Prayer
deep.b:
The prayer comes down in two forms. Matthew's (6:9–13) has seven requests and stands in the Sermon on the Mount; Luke's (11:2–4) has five and comes as Jesus' answer to a disciple's request. Luke's oldest manuscripts begin simply "Father," lack "may your will be done" and "rescue us from the evil one," and ask God to keep giving bread "each day" and to forgive "sins." Later scribes made Luke match Matthew, which is why the KJV reads almost the same in both places (see the variants).

Which is closer to Jesus? Many scholars, following Joachim Jeremias, think Luke kept the shorter length and Matthew the older wording: the church would add to a prayer of Jesus, but hardly cut it. Others think Jesus taught the prayer more than once, in different forms. The Didache, a church manual from about AD 100, gives Matthew's form with a closing praise and tells Christians to pray it three times a day (Didache 8:2–3). That is the form most churches still pray.

Luke's setting adds something Matthew's does not: the prayer is a gift from teacher to disciples, like John's prayer for his followers. It marks out who they are. Luke follows it with two lessons on how to pray it: with bold confidence, like the friend at midnight, and with trust in a Father who gives the Holy Spirit.

Luke 11:37–54 is one of the sharpest passages in the Gospels, and it has been used for centuries to paint Pharisees, and through them Jews in general, as legalists who cared only for outward ritual. Three things help a fair reading.

The setting. Jesus speaks as a guest at a Pharisee's table, among Jews, in a debate about how to keep God's law. His charges are those of a prophet: like Isaiah or Amos, he accuses people of keeping religious duties while neglecting justice (Isaiah 1:10–17; Amos 5:21–24). Jesus does not reject tithing or purity ("These you should have done," 11:42).

The Pharisees themselves. Historians such as E. P. Sanders and Jacob Neusner describe the Pharisees as a respected lay movement that tried to bring holiness into daily life. Later rabbis, their heirs, criticized hypocrites in their own ranks; the Talmud lists kinds of Pharisees who make a show of piety (Babylonian Talmud Sotah 22b). Luke himself shows Pharisees who host Jesus, warn him (13:31), defend the apostles (Acts 5:34–39) and become believers (Acts 15:5).

Luke's purpose. Luke writes for Christians, and he says plainly that the yeast of hypocrisy is a danger for disciples (12:1). The woes are a mirror for church leaders as much as a record of a quarrel.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two hosts and a guest
deep.b:
This is my own reading, not a published one I know of, though it builds on the common observation that Luke uses meals to reveal hearts. Luke 11 has two scenes of hospitality that mirror each other. In the parable (11:5–8) a man is woken at midnight by a friend who needs bread for a guest. Even if he is grumpy, he gets up and gives what is needed, and Jesus says God gives far more freely (11:13). At the end of the chapter (11:37–54) a Pharisee invites Jesus to a daytime meal in comfort, and instead of welcoming his guest he judges him for not washing.

Jesus' command to the host, "give what is inside as alms" (11:41), may be meant to answer the first scene: real cleanness looks like the friend who opens his door and gives his bread. The chapter thus moves from God as the generous friend, to a host who measures his guest by rules. If this is right, the woes are not only accusations but an invitation to become the kind of host the parable describes.

echoes: Matthew 6:9–13; Matthew 7:7–11; Matthew 12:22–45; Matthew 5:15; Matthew 6:22–23; Matthew 23:1–36; Mark 3:22–27; Exodus 8:19; Exodus 16:4; Isaiah 49:24–25; 1 Kings 10:1–13; Jonah 3:1–10; Genesis 4:8–10; 2 Chronicles 24:20–22; Numbers 19:16; Leviticus 27:30; Deuteronomy 6:5; Micah 6:8

settings.what: The Lord's Prayer
settings.to: His disciples, after one of them asked to be taught
settings.when: Somewhere on the journey to Jerusalem, right after Jesus has finished praying
settings.why: To give the disciples a prayer of their own, as John had done for his followers: a short, daily prayer that puts God's name and kingdom first and asks for bread, forgiveness and protection. Knowing that it answers a request matters: it is a gift to people who saw Jesus pray and wanted to pray like him.
settings.readers: Luke wrote for Theophilus (1:3) and the churches he stood for. Most scholars think they were mainly Gentile believers; others, such as Jacob Jervell, argue that many were Jewish believers and God-fearers. When Luke wrote is also debated (see the book's introduction). For them the prayer's short form and its "each day" fit a church praying daily over a long life, not only through a short wait for the end.
views: Many think Jesus taught the prayer more than once, and that Matthew and Luke each kept one occasion.
One prayer, placed by each evangelist
Others think the prayer came down without a setting, and Matthew put it in the Sermon on the Mount while Luke built a scene around it.

settings.what: The parable of the friend at midnight
settings.to: The disciples who had asked about prayer
settings.when: Right after the Lord's Prayer
settings.why: To give them confidence in prayer. Jesus' "Which of you...?" expects the answer "No one would refuse a friend in need." If a sleepy neighbor will give bread at midnight, God, who is no reluctant sleeper, will certainly answer those who ask. Whether the point is bold persistence or God's own honor depends on how one reads "shamelessness" (11:8).
settings.readers: Luke's readers heard a lesson they would meet again in the widow and the judge (18:1–8): pray and do not lose heart.

settings.what: Ask, look, knock
settings.to: The disciples
settings.when: Following the parable
settings.why: To turn the parable into a promise and to name the best gift. The Father who knows how to give good things will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. For disciples who will soon carry the message without Jesus' presence, this was the gift that mattered most.
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew from Acts how the Spirit had come to praying believers (Acts 1:14; 2:1–4; 4:31). In Matthew the same sayings close the Sermon on the Mount's teaching on prayer and end with "what is good" (Matthew 7:11).

settings.what: The answer to the Beelzebul charge
settings.to: The crowds, especially "some of them" who said he cast out demons by Beelzebul and others who demanded a sign
settings.when: After he drove a demon out of a man who could not speak
settings.why: To refute a dangerous accusation of sorcery and to tell the crowd what his exorcisms mean: Satan's kingdom is not divided but defeated, God's kingdom has arrived, and neutrality is impossible. In Mark the accusers are Jerusalem scribes and in Matthew Pharisees; Luke makes them people from the crowd, so the decision is put to ordinary hearers.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, who knew of Christians accused of magic (Acts 8:9–24; 13:6–12; 19:13–19), the passage separated Jesus' power from sorcery and placed it with the God of the exodus.

settings.what: The return of the unclean spirit
settings.to: The same crowd
settings.when: Continuing the Beelzebul answer
settings.why: To warn that being freed from evil is not enough; a life left empty will be filled again by something worse. Luke sets this before the blessing on those who hear and keep God's word (11:28), which is how the house is filled.
views: Luke's placement, without Matthew's closing line about "this evil generation" (Matthew 12:45), points to each hearer.
Some read it, with Matthew, as a picture of Israel's generation cleansed by John's and Jesus' preaching but not turning to God.

settings.what: Who is blessed
settings.by: A woman in the crowd, then Jesus
settings.to: Jesus, and through his answer the crowd
settings.when: While he is answering the Beelzebul charge
settings.why: The woman praises Jesus by blessing his mother, a Jewish way of honoring a son. Jesus answers that the greater blessing belongs to everyone who hears the word of God and keeps it. It continues the call of 11:23–26 to take a side and fill the house.
settings.readers: Luke's readers had read Mary's own words, "every generation will count me blessed" (1:48), and knew her as the one who kept God's words in her heart (2:19, 51). How they would have heard 11:28 is debated; see the card on this chapter.

settings.what: The sign of Jonah
settings.to: The crowds, growing larger
settings.when: In answer to those who had demanded a sign out of heaven (11:16)
settings.why: To refuse a proof on demand and to point to what was already in front of them: a messenger greater than Jonah and Solomon. Gentiles who listened to lesser messengers will condemn this generation at the judgment. Matthew sets the saying in a separate debate with scribes and Pharisees and adds the three days in the fish (Matthew 12:38–42).

settings.what: The lamp and the eye
settings.to: The crowds
settings.when: Following the sign of Jonah
settings.why: God has set the light where everyone can see it; the problem is not the lamp but the eye. A sound eye takes in the light, an evil eye sees only darkness. Matthew has the lamp saying in the Sermon on the Mount about the disciples' witness (Matthew 5:15) and the eye saying about money (Matthew 6:22–23).

settings.what: Woes on the Pharisees
settings.to: His Pharisee host and, it seems, other Pharisee guests at the meal
settings.when: At a midday meal, after the host was surprised that Jesus did not wash first
settings.why: To answer the host's silent judgment with a prophet's rebuke. The issues are practices of the Pharisees' own tradition: washing before meals, the purity of vessels, tithing garden herbs. Jesus does not reject these (11:42) but says they mean nothing without inner cleanness, alms, justice and love for God. These are rulings of a Jewish movement about how to keep the Torah in daily life, not laws of Moses binding all Israel.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers it was a warning that applied to them too: "hypocrisy" (12:1) was a danger for disciples, and 11:41's alms became a mark of Luke's churches (Acts 9:36; 10:2).
views: Many take the scene as a real occasion that Luke has filled with sayings from Jesus' teaching.
Others note that Matthew 23 places the same sayings in a public speech in the temple, and think Luke created the meal as a setting, as he often does.

settings.what: Woes on the lawyers
settings.to: The lawyers, experts in the law of Moses, present at the meal; one had protested that Jesus insulted them too
settings.when: At the same meal
settings.why: To charge the scholars who interpreted the law with burdening people without helping them, honoring dead prophets while resisting living ones, and locking up the meaning of Scripture. The words of God's Wisdom (11:49–51) set Jesus' generation at the end of the long history of rejected messengers, from Abel to Zechariah.
settings.readers: Whenever Luke wrote, his readers knew from Acts that apostles were hunted and killed as Wisdom said. If he wrote after AD 70, as many think, they had also seen the woe on the generation (11:50–51) come true in the fall of Jerusalem.

traditions.q: A woman calls Jesus' mother blessed, and he answers, "Rather, blessed are the people who hear the word of God and keep it" (11:27–28). Does this lessen the honor Christians give Mary, or explain it?
views: It explains it. Mary is blessed above all because she heard God's word and kept it; her faith came before her motherhood. Vatican II cites this passage to say that Mary faithfully did what Jesus praised (Lumen Gentium 58), and Augustine wrote that she was more blessed in receiving Christ by faith than in conceiving him in the flesh (On Holy Virginity 3). Honor and devotion to her are fitting.

It explains it. The Church reads 10:38–42 together with 11:27–28 as the Gospel at feasts of the Mother of God, hearing in the woman's cry a fulfillment of 1:48 and in Jesus' answer a description of the Theotokos, who kept the word perfectly.

It explains and limits it. The Lutheran confessions call Mary "the most blessed virgin" and mother of God (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 8.24), and grant that she prays for the church, while rejecting prayer to her as a mediator (Apology of the Augsburg Confession 21). Her blessedness, like every believer's, rests on hearing and keeping God's word, which is what this verse says.

It redirects it. Jesus turns praise away from bodily relationship to faith and obedience, which are open to all. Calvin, on this passage in his Harmony of the Evangelists, takes Jesus to be correcting a praise that rested on the flesh, while not denying that Mary was blessed. Mary is honored as a believer, but the verse gives no ground for prayer to her or veneration.

It redirects it. The highest blessing is not to be related to Jesus but to hear and obey God's word, and it is offered to every believer. Mary is a model of faith, not a mediator or an object of devotion.

title: Fear, Greed and Readiness
sum: With tens of thousands crowding around, Jesus warns his disciples against the Pharisees' hypocrisy, which will not stay hidden, and tells them not to fear those who can kill only the body. God, who does not forget a single sparrow, counts the hairs on their heads; the Holy Spirit will give them words when they are put on trial. A man asks Jesus to settle an inheritance; Jesus refuses and tells the parable of a rich fool who builds bigger barns and dies that night.

Turning to his disciples, Jesus tells them not to worry about food or clothing: God feeds the ravens and dresses the lilies, and the Father has chosen to give them the kingdom, so they can sell what they have and give alms. They must be like slaves ready for their master's return at any hour; the master will even serve them. To Peter he speaks of a manager who must be found faithful. He says he came to cast fire and faces a baptism of suffering, and that he brings division, even in families. He ends by asking the crowds why they can read the weather but not the time they are living in.
readings: Luke builds the chapter around money and security. The man who wants his inheritance, the rich fool with his barns, the ravens with no storeroom, the command to sell and give, and the manager who feeds the household all ask the same question: where is your treasure? (12:34). Luke's answer is radical: life does not come from possessions, and generosity is the way to be rich toward God.
Read as teaching on the end

From 12:35 the chapter looks ahead to the master's return, the thief at night and the judgment. Hans Conzelmann argued that Luke rewrote the tradition for a church facing the delay of the Second Coming: "My master's coming is delayed" (12:45). Others answer that Luke keeps both a living hope and a call to faithful work in the meantime.
Read as a call to courage

The chapter opens and closes with crisis: trials before synagogues and rulers (12:11), fire and division (12:49–53), a court case on the road (12:58). Jesus' "Stop being afraid" (12:7, 32) runs through it. For disciples who would face persecution, it is a chapter about whom to fear, and why not to fear anything else.

views.H: The world behind the chapter is agricultural and economic: inheritance disputes settled by teachers, rich landowners storing harvests to sell when prices rose, cheap sparrows in the market, wildflowers burned as oven fuel, managers who were themselves slaves, debtors handed to a court officer and jailed.
views.C: Luke combines material shared with Matthew (Matthew 10:26–33; 6:19–34; 24:43–51; 10:34–36; 5:25–26) with his own: the inheritance request, the rich fool, the master who serves, Peter's question, degrees of punishment, fire and baptism. Conzelmann's thesis that Luke postponed the end and created a "period of the church" has been influential and much criticized.
views.L: The chapter alternates audiences: disciples (12:1–12), someone from the crowd (12:13–21), disciples (12:22–53), crowds (12:54–59). Luke's parable characters talk to themselves (12:17–19, 45). Key words repeat: "soul/life" (12:19–23), "treasure" (12:21, 33–34), "ready" (12:20, 40, 47), "fear" (12:4–7, 32).
views.J: Much of the chapter echoes Jewish wisdom: Ecclesiastes and Sirach on the folly of hoarding, the Psalms on God feeding the ravens, Daniel's kingdom given to God's people, Micah's divided families, the Law's distinction between knowing and unknowing sin. "The nations of the world" is a Jewish phrase. Jesus' disciples are pictured as Israel's "little flock."
views.T: Basil the Great preached on the rich fool during a famine (about AD 368), and Ambrose and John Chrysostom made the parable a standard text for almsgiving. 12:33 shaped monastic and Franciscan poverty. 12:48 ("to whom much is given") became a proverb of responsibility in Western culture.

deep.h: The rich fool and Luke's teaching on wealth
deep.b:
Only Luke tells this parable, and it fits his whole Gospel, which pronounces woe on the rich (6:24), sends a rich ruler away sad (18:23), and praises Zacchaeus for giving half his goods to the poor (19:8). The rich man in the parable does nothing illegal. His land produces a big crop, and he plans to store it. His folly lies elsewhere.

He is alone. He talks only to himself and his soul. No family, workers or neighbors appear. Kenneth Bailey notes how strange this would seem in a village where such decisions were talked over with everyone.

He thinks he owns his life. God's word "they demand your soul back" uses the language of a loan called in. Wisdom writers had said the same: Ecclesiastes on leaving one's toil to whoever comes after (Ecclesiastes 2:18–21), and Sirach on the man who says "now I will eat from my goods" and dies (Sirach 11:18–19).

He is not rich toward God. Luke defines this at once: sell, give alms, and have a treasure in heaven (12:33). The church fathers pressed the point. Basil of Caesarea, preaching in a famine, told the rich that the bread they stored belonged to the hungry and the coat in their closet to the naked.

The churches differ on whether Jesus' command to sell is for all or for some; their views are compared at Matthew 19:21 and Acts 4.

The parables of 12:35–48 picture the time between Jesus' going and his return as a household waiting at night. Three images build on one another: servants with lamps lit for a master coming back from a wedding (12:35–38), a householder who did not know when the thief would come (12:39–40), and a manager who must feed the household while the master is away (12:42–48).

Luke's version adds two things. First, the astonishing master who serves his slaves (12:37), a picture of the messianic banquet and of Jesus himself, who at the Last Supper calls himself "like the one who waits on tables" (22:27). Second, Peter's question (12:41), which turns the last parable toward leaders: those set over God's household will answer for how they treated it (12:45–48).

Scholars debate how Luke saw the timing. Hans Conzelmann read "My master's coming is delayed" (12:45) as Luke's answer to a church disappointed that the end had not come. Others point out that Luke also says the master may come at any watch of the night (12:38) and that the call is readiness, not calculation (Acts 1:6–8). The traditions' views on the Second Coming are compared at Matthew 24.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three barns
deep.b:
Commentators already link the rich fool's barns (12:18) with the ravens that have "no storeroom and no barn, yet God feeds them" (12:24). The word apothēkē, "barn," ties the parable to the teaching on worry. Matthew 6:26 also mentions barns, but only Luke has the two passages side by side. That much is standard.

My own suggestion goes one step further. The "pouches that never get old" and the "endless treasure in the heavens" (12:33) look like a third barn, Luke's answer to the first two: the rich man's barns are useless the night he dies, the ravens need none, and the disciple builds the only storehouse that lasts by giving. Commentators often tie 12:33 back to the parable as well; what I add is the idea that Luke built the three as a deliberate sequence, from a barn that fails, through no barn at all, to a barn in heaven.

echoes: Matthew 10:19–20; Matthew 10:26–36; Matthew 12:31–32; Matthew 6:19–34; Matthew 24:42–51; Matthew 16:2–3; Matthew 5:25–26; Mark 8:15; Mark 3:28–29; Mark 10:38–39; Exodus 2:14; Exodus 12:11; Deuteronomy 21:17; Numbers 15:27–31; Job 38:41; Psalm 147:9; Psalm 14:1; Ecclesiastes 2:18–21; Ecclesiastes 8:15; Isaiah 40:11; Daniel 7:27; Micah 7:6; Sirach 11:18–19; Acts 4:8; Acts 6:10

settings.what: Warnings and courage for the disciples
settings.to: His disciples first, with a vast crowd overhearing
settings.when: Right after the hostile meal of 11:37–54, as the crowds swell to tens of thousands
settings.why: To prepare the disciples for the opposition they had just seen: avoid the Pharisees' hypocrisy, since everything hidden will come out; do not fear people who can only kill the body; trust the God who counts hairs; stand up for Jesus in public; and rely on the Holy Spirit at trial. Matthew has most of these sayings in the mission speech to the Twelve (Matthew 10:17–33).
settings.readers: Some of Luke's readers had stood before synagogues and magistrates. Acts would show the promise of 12:11–12 kept by Peter, Stephen and Paul.

settings.what: The refusal to divide an inheritance
settings.to: A man from the crowd, then the crowd ("them")
settings.when: As Jesus is teaching the disciples
settings.why: The man wanted a respected teacher to rule in his favor in a family dispute. Jesus refuses the role of property judge and names the real problem: greed. Under the Law, inheritance followed set rules (Deuteronomy 21:17; Numbers 27:1–11); the question Jesus raises is not who is legally right, but what a person's life consists of.

settings.what: The parable of the rich fool
settings.to: The man who asked about the inheritance, and the crowd
settings.when: Right after the warning against greed
settings.why: To show what greed looks like from God's side: a man who plans for many years and has one night left. It shocked hearers who admired wise saving, and pointed them to being rich toward God, which Luke spells out in 12:33.
settings.readers: Luke's readers included well-off believers (1:3; Acts 17:12), and the parable was one of many in Luke that called them to share. Only Luke has it.

settings.what: Do not worry; seek the kingdom
settings.to: His disciples
settings.when: Following the rich fool
settings.why: To free disciples from anxiety about food and clothing, the opposite of the rich man's anxiety about storage. God feeds and clothes his creatures; the Father has chosen to give them the kingdom; so they can afford to be generous. Matthew has the same teaching in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:19–34), but Luke ends with a direct command to sell and give alms.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, many of them poor, the words gave courage; for the wealthier, a summons. Acts 2:44–45 and 4:32–37 show the first church living it.

settings.what: The parables of the waiting slaves and the thief
settings.to: His disciples
settings.when: Continuing the same teaching
settings.why: To call for readiness at every hour, since the master's return is certain but its time unknown. The promise that the master will serve his watchful slaves gives the waiting joy as well as urgency. Matthew sets the thief saying in the discourse on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24:43–44).
views: Most read the master's return as Christ's return in glory.
Some apply it to the coming of judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus' hearers would live to see.
Many preachers, following 12:20, apply it to the unknown hour of each person's death.

settings.what: The faithful and unfaithful manager
settings.to: Peter, who asked whether the parable was for the disciples or for all, and the disciples
settings.when: After the parables of readiness
settings.why: To answer Peter by pointing to those put in charge of others: the manager who feeds the household will be rewarded, the one who abuses it judged, and more is asked of those given more. The words fit the Twelve, the future leaders of the church. Matthew has the parable without Peter's question and without the closing sayings on degrees of punishment (Matthew 24:45–51).
settings.readers: For Luke's readers it was a word to church leaders, the "managers" and overseers of Acts 20:28 and the letters.

settings.what: Fire, baptism and division
settings.to: His disciples
settings.when: At the end of the teaching on readiness, on the road to Jerusalem
settings.why: To reveal what Jesus himself faces and what following him will cost: he longs for the fire of God's work to blaze, must first go through the baptism of his death, and brings a peace that divides even families. It warned disciples not to expect easy acceptance at home. Matthew has the division saying in the mission discourse (Matthew 10:34–36).

settings.what: Reading the times and settling on the way
settings.to: The crowds
settings.when: Turning from the disciples to the crowds
settings.why: To shame the crowds into seeing what was happening in front of them: they read clouds and winds but not God's moment. The court picture urges them to settle their case with God now, on the road, before judgment. Matthew uses the court saying in the Sermon on the Mount for reconciling with a brother (Matthew 5:25–26), so the same picture serves two purposes.

title: A Year More, a Woman Freed, a City Mourned
sum: People tell Jesus about Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices. He refuses to say they were worse sinners, or the eighteen crushed by the tower at Siloam, and warns that all will perish unless they repent. He tells a parable of a fig tree that has borne nothing for three years and is given one more year of care. In a synagogue on the Sabbath he straightens a woman bent double for eighteen years; when the synagogue leader objects, Jesus answers that a daughter of Abraham must be freed from Satan's bond on the Sabbath of all days.

He compares God's kingdom to a mustard seed that becomes a tree and yeast hidden in flour. Traveling on toward Jerusalem, he is asked whether few will be saved. He answers with a narrow door that will be locked, people outside claiming they knew him, and a feast with Abraham and people from every direction. Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him. He calls Herod a fox, says no prophet should die outside Jerusalem, and laments over the city he longed to gather like a bird gathering her young.
readings: Read as a call to repentance

The chapter is framed by warnings: perish unless you repent (13:3, 5), a fig tree given one last year (13:6–9), a door that will be locked (13:25), a house left abandoned (13:35). God's patience is real, and so is its limit. The healing of the bent woman shows what repentance opens the way to: release and joy.

Many scholars read the chapter as Jesus' warning to his own generation in Judea and Galilee. Pilate's killing in the temple courts and a collapsing tower foreshadow the Roman war of AD 66–70, when Jews died in the temple and under falling buildings. The fruitless fig tree and the abandoned house point to Jerusalem's fall. Luke, writing after that war, saw the warnings fulfilled.
Read as a picture of the kingdom

In the middle of warnings stand pictures of hope: a woman set free, a seed that grows into a tree for the birds, yeast that raises the whole batch, a feast with people from east and west. The kingdom begins small and hidden and ends in a great gathering, but the guests are not always the ones who expected to be there.

views.H: Pontius Pilate's record in Josephus and Philo makes a killing in the temple courts believable, though no other source records it. Siloam was in Jerusalem's southeast corner by the Pool of Siloam. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea, had already killed John the Baptist. A synagogue leader ran local Sabbath services. Fig trees were commonly planted in vineyards.
views.C: Luke's own material dominates: the Galileans and Siloam, the fig tree, the bent woman, the Herod warning. The mustard seed, yeast, narrow door and lament over Jerusalem are shared with Matthew. Many scholars see the fig tree parable as Luke's replacement for Mark's cursing of the fig tree, and the lament's placement before the entry into Jerusalem as Luke's arrangement.
views.L: The chapter turns on the number eighteen (13:4, 11, 16) and on paired stories: men and women (the mustard seed and the yeast), a tree spared and a woman straightened. Luke reminds the reader of the journey (13:22) and the destination (13:33–35). The word "must" (dei, 13:14, 16, 33) contrasts human rules with God's purpose.
views.J: The Sabbath dispute is among Jews about how to honor the Sabbath, and Jesus argues from accepted practice. "Daughter of Abraham" honors a woman as a full member of the covenant people. Luke's Pharisees warn Jesus to save his life (13:31). The lament over Jerusalem is the grief of a prophet for his own city, like Jeremiah's, not a rejection of the Jewish people; it ends in a hope, "Blessed is the one who comes."
views.T: The fig tree given another year has been a favorite Lenten text about God's patience. Gregory the Great preached on the fig tree and the bent woman together, reading the woman as the soul bowed down by sin and raised by Christ (Homilies on the Gospels 31). The hen gathering her chicks inspired medieval devotion to Christ as mother, as in Anselm's prayer to Saint Paul and Julian of Norwich.

deep.b:
Two disasters frame Jesus' answer: a political killing (Pilate's soldiers cutting down Galilean pilgrims at their sacrifices) and an accident (a tower falling on eighteen people). Both raise the old question of whether suffering is punishment for sin. Job's friends said yes; the book of Job says it is not that simple (Job 42:7), and the disciples ask the same question in John 9:2.

Jesus' answer has two halves. First, no: the victims were not worse sinners or worse "debtors" than anyone else. This forbids reading every tragedy as a verdict on the victims, a lesson often needed after earthquakes, epidemics and wars. Second, everyone needs to repent. Disasters are not explanations but reminders that life is fragile and judgment is real.

Many scholars, such as N. T. Wright, read the words "perish the same way" more concretely, as a warning to Jesus' own generation: if Israel chose the path of armed revolt against Rome, more Galileans would die in the temple courts and more Jerusalemites under falling walls. In AD 70 that is what happened, as Josephus describes. Luke, writing after the war, knew it.

deep.h: Jerusalem, Herod and the prophet's road (13:31–35)
deep.b:
The chapter ends with a warning and a lament. Some Pharisees tell Jesus to leave Herod Antipas's territory because Herod wants him dead. Luke does not say whether they were friends or agents; Luke's Pharisees are a mixed group, and nothing in the text accuses these men of lying. Jesus' reply is defiant: Herod is a "fox," a sly and petty ruler, and he cannot change God's timetable. Jesus will finish his work and go to Jerusalem, because that is where prophets die.

Then he speaks to the city itself. The lament gathers up the history of 11:47–51, the prophets killed and stoned, and pictures Jesus as a mother bird longing to shelter her young, an image the Psalms use for God. "Your house is abandoned to you" recalls Jeremiah's warnings before the first destruction of the temple. Yet it closes with Psalm 118:26, the pilgrims' welcome.

Christian readers have sometimes used this passage to claim that God abandoned the Jewish people. The text does not say that. It is the lament of a Jewish prophet over Jerusalem, it ends with a welcome still to be spoken, and Luke's next chapters show Jesus weeping over the city (19:41–44). Whether the final line promises a future turning of Israel to its Messiah is debated; see the note at 13:35 and the card at Isaiah 59:20.

deep.title: Claude's theory: eighteen years, and a year of release
deep.b:
This is my own reading. The number eighteen appears three times in this chapter and nowhere else in Luke: the eighteen killed at Siloam (13:4) and the woman bound for eighteen years (13:11, 16). Commentators have noted the repetition but usually treat it as chance. I suggest Luke keeps it on purpose to pair the two scenes: eighteen people for whom no time was left, and a woman for whom eighteen years of bondage end in a day.

Between them stands the fig tree given "one year more" (13:8). Jesus' first sermon announced "a year of the Lord's welcome" and release for the captives (4:18–19, from Isaiah 61:1–2), and the healing happens on the Sabbath, the day the Law ties to release from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). Read together, the three scenes say that Jesus' ministry is the year of grace: a last year for the tree, release for the woman, and a warning for everyone else that the time is short.

echoes: Matthew 13:31–33; Mark 4:30–32; Matthew 7:13–14; Matthew 7:22–23; Matthew 25:10–12; Matthew 8:11–12; Matthew 19:30; Matthew 23:37–39; Mark 11:12–14; Isaiah 5:1–7; Micah 7:1; Leviticus 19:23–25; Deuteronomy 5:12–15; Psalm 6:8; Psalm 107:3; Isaiah 43:5–6; Isaiah 25:6; Psalm 91:4; Psalm 118:26; Jeremiah 12:7; Jeremiah 22:5; Genesis 18:6; Daniel 4:12; Ezekiel 17:23

Parable of the barren fig tree

settings.what: The Galileans and the tower of Siloam
settings.to: People in the crowd who brought him news of Pilate's killing of Galileans
settings.when: Right after his warning to settle with God while on the road (12:54–59)
settings.why: To stop his hearers from treating victims as worse sinners and themselves as safe. Both disasters become a call to repent before a greater judgment. The bearers of the news may have wanted Jesus to condemn Pilate, or to comment on the Galileans' guilt; he does neither.
views: Others read it as a warning that an unrepentant nation would meet the same violent end in the revolt of AD 66–70.

settings.what: The parable of the fig tree
settings.to: The same hearers
settings.when: Following the call to repent
settings.why: To show both the patience and the urgency of God: the tree has failed, and judgment is deserved, but a gardener pleads for one more year with special care. The hearers are given time, but not forever.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, who did not have Mark's cursing of the fig tree in this Gospel, met here a gentler but no less serious picture of Israel and of every hearer.
views: Many read the tree as Israel or Jerusalem, as in the prophets, given a last chance in Jesus' ministry.
Others read it as a picture of any person whose life bears no fruit of repentance (3:8–9).

settings.what: The Sabbath healing and the dispute that followed
settings.by: Jesus, the synagogue leader, then Jesus
settings.to: The woman; the synagogue leader speaking to the crowd; Jesus' reply to him and to all who agreed with him ("Hypocrites")
settings.when: On a Sabbath, while Jesus was teaching in a synagogue on the journey
settings.why: The leader applied a reasonable rule of Sabbath practice: treatment of a long illness that is not life-threatening can wait for a weekday. The Torah's command ("six days you shall work") binds all Israel; how it applied to healing was a matter of interpretation. Jesus answers from accepted practice, watering animals, and from the Sabbath's purpose as a day of release (Deuteronomy 5:15): if an animal may be untied, how much more a daughter of Abraham bound by Satan.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the Sabbath was a live question between Jewish and Gentile believers (Acts 15; Romans 14:5–6).

settings.what: The parable of the mustard seed
settings.to: The people in the synagogue, it seems ("So he said")
settings.when: Right after the healing and the crowd's joy
settings.why: To say that the release they had just seen was the small beginning of God's great kingdom, which will grow to shelter many. In Mark and Matthew the parable belongs to the lakeside parables (Mark 4:30–32; Matthew 13:31–32); Luke ties it to the healing.

settings.what: The parable of the yeast
settings.to: The same hearers
settings.when: Immediately after the mustard seed
settings.why: To pair a man's work in a garden with a woman's work in a kitchen: the kingdom works hidden and unseen until it has transformed the whole. Matthew has the same pair (Matthew 13:31–33).

settings.what: The narrow door
settings.to: Someone who asked whether few would be saved, and the people traveling with him ("them")
settings.when: On the road through towns and villages toward Jerusalem
settings.why: To turn a speculative question into an urgent one: do not ask how many, strain to get in yourself while the door is open. Acquaintance with Jesus will not be enough; people from every direction will sit at the feast while those who assumed they belonged are outside. Matthew scatters these sayings through the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 7:13–14; Matthew 7:22–23), the centurion story (Matthew 8:11–12) and the ten young women (Matthew 25:10–12).
settings.readers: Luke's readers, Gentile believers who had come "from east and west," heard both a welcome and a warning against assuming their own place.

settings.what: The answer to Herod
settings.to: Some Pharisees who warned him that Herod Antipas wanted to kill him; through them, Herod
settings.when: "Just then" (13:31), still in Herod's territory on the journey
settings.why: To say that no ruler could cut short his work or change its destination: he will finish his exorcisms and healings and go on to Jerusalem, where prophets die. Only Luke has the scene.
views: Some take the Pharisees as well-meaning, like Gamaliel later (Acts 5:34–39).
Others think they wanted him out of Galilee, perhaps with Herod's approval.

settings.what: The lament over Jerusalem
settings.to: Jerusalem, addressed from a distance, in the hearing of those with him
settings.when: On the journey, before he has entered the city
settings.why: To grieve over the city that kills prophets and refuses to be gathered, to warn that its house will be left to itself, and to leave open the welcome of Psalm 118:26. Matthew puts the lament at the end of Jesus' last speech in the temple (Matthew 23:37–39); Luke places it before the entry, where the disciples will cry "Blessed is the King who comes in the Lord's name!" (19:38).
settings.readers: If Luke wrote after AD 70, his readers knew the city had fallen (19:41–44; 21:20–24). Either way, the lament taught them to read Jerusalem's refusal and its fate with grief, not triumph.
